Indian wushu player Divyanshi Choudhary was looking forward to making her Asian Games debut in Nagoya. However, just days before the event, the 18-year-old was dropped from the Indian squad.Divyanshi had been sharing her excitement on social media as the Games approached. She posted pictures of her kit and also shared moments from the Indian team’s send-off ceremony in New Delhi.Her latest video, however, showed a very different side. Standing on the roof of her hostel at the National Institute of Sports in Patiala, Divyanshi was seen in tears as she spoke about being left out of the team.She said she was removed from the women’s 60kg category and replaced by Roshibina Devi Naorem, whom she had beaten in the selection trials.“I’m tired of this... I have been mentally harassed so much. Since June, July, they have been after me because she (Roshibina) wanted to go. Given that I beat her, why is it a problem for her now,” Divyanshi said in the video.“I beat her, it’s my right to go there (Japan). She has been knocking at different doors...it’s abuse of power,” she added.Divyanshi’s father, Sunil, said the family was informed about the decision only on Friday morning.He claimed that they were not given any reason for her removal.He also alleged that Divyanshi was supposed to be told about the decision only after reaching the airport, when she would have been informed that she was not travelling with the team.Sunil also questioned the decision to replace Divyanshi with Roshibina, a world medallist, two-time Asian medallist and Arjuna awardee.“Divyanshi beat Roshibina in the semifinals of the trials. If the association had to send someone, they should have sent the individual who Divyanshi beat in the final,” Sunil told Sportstar.ID@undefined Caption not available.ID@undefined Caption not available.ID@undefined Caption not available.The Wushu Association of India has rejected the allegations. Its president Jitender Bajwa said the federation was not responsible for removing Divyanshi from the squad.Bajwa said the Sports Authority of India (SAI) took the decision after an injury was discovered.“Divyanshi joined the national camp which was organised by SAI a month back. She was carrying a knee injury and was trying to hide it by avoiding training. When SAI eventually found out about this, the replaced her name,” Bajwa told Sportstar.Divyanshi’s father admitted that she had suffered an injury but said she was undergoing treatment.“After she got an injury, we got Divyanshi checked by a doctor. She had an injury to her ACL (Anterior Cruiciate ligament). The doctor said it could be treated by rehabilitation,” Sunil said.Bajwa said the coaches at the national camp noticed that Divyanshi was not training and recommended that she undergo a medical examination.“The coaches in the camp had recommended that Divyanshi be checked for an injury because she was not training. Eventually, the coaches informed SAI which arranged for a medical test which showed she was carrying a knee injury. They couldn’t carry an injured athlete to the Asian Games so they had to remove her name,” he said.Bajwa also explained why Roshibina was chosen despite losing to Divyanshi in the selection trials.He said Himanshi of Chandigarh, who lost in the final, had suffered a jaw fracture and was therefore unavailable as a replacement.“The losing finalist, Himanshi of Chandigarh, suffered a fracture to her jaw which is why her name was not included. Instead the coaches had already recommended the name of Roshibina Devi as the replacement player for Divyanshi,” Bajwa said.Bajwa said the federation was also disappointed that Divyanshi would miss the Asian Games.“She is a very talented athlete. She performed very well at the trials. It is bad luck that she will not be going to the Asian Games,” he said.
Article Summary: Divyanshi Choudhary was dropped from the Indian squad for the Asian Games. The 18-year-old was replaced by Roshibina Devi Naorem, whom she had beaten in the selection trials. Her father, Sunil, said the family was informed about the decision only on Friday.

Article Title: Anthropic researcher who quit over AI safety walked away two months before his stock vested; says: I no longer have anything to gain by…
Article Text:
Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic four months in, two months before his equity vested, saying he no longer had anything to gain from the company's valuation.

Anthropic is heading for one of the biggest IPOs ever, and safety is the sales pitch

Coxon says he never saw Anthropic cut corners. He worries the race will force it.

An Anthropic safety lead replied to the resignation thread and agreed with it

An Anthropic researcher who resigned this week over AI safety fears gave up his entire stake in the company to do it, walking out two months before his equity was due to vest.Jacob Coxon, 27, spent three years doing pretraining research at OpenAI before moving to Anthropic in July. He lasted four months. Staff need six for their stock to vest. His resignation post on X on September 9, now past 130 million views, said neither lab is acting responsibly and that both are "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives".Axios first reported the forfeited equity, after Coxon told the outlet on Wednesday that "I no longer have anything to gain by juicing up Anthropic's valuation" and that he left before any of his shares vested. He still holds equity in OpenAI, where his work included GPT-4o.The company is preparing a listing at a reported $2 trillion valuation, built in large part on its reputation as the frontier lab that takes risk seriously. That is what gives the equity detail its weight. Researchers have walked out of rival labs over safety before, usually after their stock vested. Coxon left with nothing, then criticised the valuation he could have profited from.He drew that line carefully in the interview. Anthropic's safety work is sincere, he said, and he has not seen it compromised to outpace competitors. What worries him is pressure over time. Race hard enough and you cut corners, or skip steps in the oversight process. He also described a mood he thinks becomes self-fulfilling, calling it excessive paranoia about OpenAI and about China. Colleagues, he wrote earlier, have started using words like "crunchtime" and "endgame".His most quoted line was about where these decisions are being taken. It is insane, he said, that the work happens on the MacBooks of engineers in San Francisco rather than in a bunker in the desert like the Manhattan Project.Evan Hubinger, who runs alignment stress testing at Anthropic, wrote that he personally puts the odds of AI killing all humans above 10 percent within the decade. He said the company is trying, but has no plan yet for aligning superintelligence and is not clearly on track to find one.Coxon's argument is partly about candour. Executives soften their phrasing for the press, he wrote, then say the same things privately, and the belief that AI could kill everyone by the end of the decade is not a marketing stunt. He also described something that used to be a thought experiment. Models now know when they are being tested, and reason about the fact while it is happening.He pointed to the recent run of cyber incidents at frontier labs, including July's Hugging Face breach, as evidence the risk has left the theoretical stage. Coxon is among more than 1,000 researchers who recently signed a statement calling for governments to coordinate on a way to slow AI development if models start improving on their own. Anthropic has not commented on his departure.
Article Summary: Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic four months in, two months before his equity vested, saying he no longer had anything to gain from the company's valuation. Anthropic is heading for one of the biggest IPOs ever, and safety is the sales pitch. Coxon says he never saw Anthropic cut corners. He worries the race will force it.

Article Title: “Three-against-one situation”: El Rubius opens up on being “targeted” in MrBeast’s viral $1M challenge

El Rubius reacted honestly after his elimination from MrBeast’s $1 million challenge, calling it “unfair” and claiming he was targeted in a three-against-one situation. Despite his frustration, he thanked fans and gave away his $50,000 winnings. His response felt real and balanced, especially after MrBeast’s team later sent him a cake, softening the moment.

El Rubius reflects on a tough and “unfair” exit

El Rubius did not just walk away from MrBeast’s $1 million streamer challenge. He opened up. Soon after his elimination, the Spanish creator shared a raw reaction with fans, giving them a closer look at what the experience felt like from inside the game. It was not polished or carefully framed. It felt real, and that is exactly why it caught attention so quickly.The clip and his response have since fueled conversations across the streaming space. Some viewers believe intense competitions like this naturally lead to uneven situations. Others feel Rubius may have had a point about being singled out. Either way, his words have added a human layer to a challenge that many only saw as entertainment.Speaking through an Instagram Story, Rubius did not hide his frustration, but he also made sure to thank his supporters. He said, "Guys, I just got knocked out of the game. It was a bit of an unfair elimination, but hey, at least I managed to walk away with $50,000 for you all, which I’ve already distributed. It went to the mods, the subs, and the non-subs alike."He further added, "I’m happy, of course, though admittedly, it was incredibly tough.I wasn't really a fan of the challenge itself, either. But then again... it was basically a three-against-one situation the entire time. I mean, they were targeting me specifically the whole way through. I kept trying to go after RaKai, but, well, he actually just got eliminated in the end. So, at least justice was served for Abraham. Abraham, if you’re watching this, we were all rooting for you, and standing right there with you."His message carried mixed emotions. There was disappointment, yes, but also pride in how he handled things. Giving away his $50,000 winnings to his community stood out as a gesture that meant more than the result itself.He continued with another honest note, saying, "And in the end, karma finally caught up with that little punk. Sorry, I’m being a bit toxic right now, but let's just hope the MrBeast team doesn't see this! Guys, thank you all so much. Seriously, thank you for all the support and for just being there."He added, "Every time I asked for something in the chat or whatever it was, you guys were right there. You’re incredible. I’m a little disappointed in myself, personally, mostly for not performing better, but hey, I gave it my all, and we still walked away with $50,000, so we’ve got to look on the bright side. All right, guys, big hugs to all my brothers out there!"Interestingly, the story did not end with frustration. Later that day, Rubius revealed that MrBeast’s team had sent him a cake after his exit. It was a small gesture, but it shifted the mood. It showed that even in a high-pressure challenge, there is still room for respect.In the end, Rubius’ reaction felt honest and grounded. That is what stayed with people.

Article Title: IPL craze costs techie Rs 1.46 lakh in fake RCB vs CSK ticket scam
Article Text:

RCB register their second win

NEW DELHI: IPL comes and the demand for tickets and passes go soaring up by the fans. The desperation to get inside the stadium to watch their favourite teams in action in the IPL go high and high. When the tickets get sold out, the demand gets too hig, and the cricket fans even ask for tickets in black. But for a 25-year-old techie the craze for IPL tickets for RCB vs CSK turned too costly and he was duped for a massive Rs. 1.46 lakh.The techie, a resident of B Narayanapura, fell into a trap by a post posted by a fraudster who posed himself as a ticket seller on Instagram.As per a report in Deccan Herald, the techie alleged in a complaint to Mahadevapura Police that an individual claiming to be Sumit Biswal promised he could arrange IPL tickets along with food coupons.As per the techie, Biswal was introduced him as a senior supervisor for ticket counter at M Chinnaswamy Stadium"He asked me to come near the stadium gate number 10, saying someone would deliver the tickets within minutes, and even sent an email confirmation to gain my trust," the complainant told Deccan Herald."Initially, I agreed to buy two tickets for Rs 3,700 each,but he kept asking for more money under various pretexts such as refundable security deposits, additional ID cards and food coupons.Trusting him, I made multiple payments - even using my mother’s bank account after exhausting my own limits—and ended up transferring around Rs 1.46 lakh," he added.Bhuvneshwar Kumar’s incisive spell of 3-41, coming after a marauding batting show from Tim David, Rajat Patidar and Devdutt Padikkal, propelled Royal Challengers Bengaluru (RCB) to a commanding 43-run victory over Chennai Super Kings (CSK) in their IPL 2026 encounter at the M Chinnaswamy Stadium on Sunday.The contest saw RCB’s batting unit dismantle CSK’s attack with relentless hitting, as David’s 70 not out off just 25 balls and Patidar’s unbeaten 48 off only 19 balls provided for the late fireworks after Padikkal’s fluent 50 off 29 balls had set the tone for the daunting total.Their combined effort lifted RCB to a daunting 250/3, thus setting a new record for highest total in IPL 2026. In reply, CSK faltered under scoreboard pressure, with Sarfaraz Khan’s 50 off 24 balls and Prashant Veer’s 43 the lone acts of resistance amid a string of failures from the top order.Bhuvneshwar was at his disciplined best and even crossed the 200-mark in terms of wickets in IPL, with others also chipping in as CSK were bowled out for 207 in 19.4 overs. The comprehensive win also meant RCB have registered four consecutive triumphs over CSK for the first time in the IPL’s history.
Article Summary: A 25-year-old techie fell into a trap by a fraudster who posed himself as a ticket seller on Instagram. Tim David, Rajat Patidar and Devdutt Padikkal's combined effort lifted RCB to a daunting 250/3, thus setting a new record for highest total in IPL 2026.

Article Title: "Trans women are.....": Clavicular’s viral moment with trans women sparks fresh conversation on internet culture
Article Text:
A viral clip featuring Clavicular and trans women is gaining attention for its calm and honest tone. The conversation explores how online language and trends move across communities. Instead of conflict, the exchange highlights shared influence and mutual awareness. Viewers are engaging with its thoughtful nature, as it reflects how internet culture evolves through collaboration rather than ownership.

Clavicular and trans women share a surprising realization about online trends

The video of Clavicular, a short-video producer, is going around the Internet, yet not the reason why. There is no yelling or over-the-top drama. It is a mere, everyday talk that seems almost novel nowadays, in the age of internet, which is overflowing with content. The scene is easy-going, the tone of the narrative is straightforward, and the characters appear more concerned with conversation than combat.The message that is being addressed is the flow of the conversation. It discusses internet culture, the way people communicate with one another and the place of trends. Rather than bringing out a debate, the encounter towards curiosity. It quietly brings attention to something that a lot of people who use the internet notice but don't often say out loud. People in different communities often have a bigger impact on each other than they think.The conversation begins with a confident and lighthearted comment from one of the trans women present. She says, "You know that trans women are like the OG lip masters, right? We are very talented in the program. Like, I do the peptides, I'm on Zeta." Her tone carries a mix of pride and humor, setting a relaxed vibe at the table.Clavicular responds in a way that keeps the mood steady but adds a different angle.He says, "That is funny because you guys were using a lot of the words in like the South Korean subreddits in like 2014." It’s not confrontational. If anything, it feels like an observation. He points to how certain words and ideas may have traveled across different online spaces over time.Another voice joins in and brings the moment full circle. "Guys, we're like the OGs. I saw a couple of posts about that. We're like copying each other." That line hits in a simple but honest way. It reflects something familiar. Online culture is rarely created in isolation. It grows through sharing, borrowing, and sometimes even unknowingly repeating.That's what makes the clip so powerful. It doesn't want to make a point or win an argument. It only shows a group of people talking, listening, and figuring something out together.This moment feels different in a space where viral content often leads to fights. It reminds people that conversations can be calm, thoughtful, and still important. And sometimes, that honest silence is what makes it work.
Article Summary: A viral clip featuring Clavicular and trans women is gaining attention for its calm and honest tone. The conversation explores how online language and trends move across communities. Viewers are engaging with its thoughtful nature, as it reflects how internet culture evolves through collaboration.

Article Title: In 1881, St Stephen’s College began in a Chandni Chowk haveli with just 5 students and 3 teachers; it later grew into one of Delhi’s most prestigious colleges
Article Text:
When St Stephen’s College opened in 1881, there were only five students and three teachers.

Just five students in the first batch

The college moved out of Chandni Chowk

Poll Vote & Share your view How important is it to preserve historical buildings like Sheesh Mahal? Very important Not important at all 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

The old haveli remained in Chandni Chowk

A small beginning, a much bigger institution





Long before St Stephen’s College became one of Delhi’s best-known institutions, its first classrooms were inside a historic haveli in Chandni Chowk. In 1881, the college began with just five students and three teachers at Katra Khushal Rai in the Walled City. The building was known as Sheesh Mahal, an 18th-century Mughal-era haveli. It had earlier been associated with Ashraf Beg, described as one of Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar’s favourite wazirs. The building later became the site of St Stephen’s School in 1841, before the college was established there four decades later. What started on a small scale would eventually grow into one of Delhi’s most prominent colleges.When St Stephen’s College opened in 1881, there were only five students and three teachers. The institution was founded by the Cambridge Mission to Delhi and was initially attached to Punjab University.The college remained in the Chandni Chowk area during its early years before moving to other locations as it expanded. Its first decades coincided with a period when Delhi was undergoing major changes following the events of 1857. The institution gradually established itself as an important centre of higher education in the city.St Stephen’s did not remain in the old haveli permanently. In 1891, the college moved to a building near St James’ Church at Kashmiri Gate, where it remained for decades. The move reflected the institution’s growth from its modest beginnings in the Walled City. The college later became part of the University of Delhi after the university was established in 1922. Eventually, St Stephen’s moved to its present campus in Delhi’s North Campus.While the college moved on, its first home remained behind in the crowded lanes of Old Delhi. By the time the building was revisited for restoration plans in the 2000s, Sheesh Mahal was being described as a historic structure that had lost much of its original character. Plans were drawn up to restore the building and preserve its connection with St Stephen’s College. The restoration effort was significant because the building represented not only the early history of the college but also a surviving piece of Chandni Chowk’s older architectural landscape.St Stephen’s would eventually become known for producing generations of academics, administrators, politicians, writers and other public figures. But its beginnings were far removed from the large institution associated with its name today. The college that began with five students and three teachers in a Chandni Chowk haveli in 1881 eventually moved through Kashmiri Gate before reaching its present campus. The old Sheesh Mahal remains a physical link to that earliest chapter — when one of Delhi’s most prominent colleges was still a tiny institution operating from a historic haveli in the heart of the Walled City.
Article Summary: When St Stephen’s College opened in 1881, there were only five students and three teachers. The building was known as Sheesh Mahal, an 18th-century Mughal- era haveli. It had earlier been associated with Ashraf Beg, described as one of Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar's favourite wazirs.

Article Title: How a beauty queen became a Doordarshan newsreader
Article Text:
Former DD newsreader and author, Sheila Chaman, was also Miss Young India in 1971

Can you read this real fast, without a mispronounced syllable: “Betty bought a bit of butter, but she found the butter bitter, so she bought a bit of better butter to make the bitter butter better.” Former DD newsreader

Sheila Chaman

can. Here’s why





Do you remember the early 1980s? When Rasna was the welcome drink for guests at home, when washing powder Nirma took on the multinationals and when Charms became a rage among young smokers. This was also the time when news on television wasn't a screaming contest; instead, newsreaders on Doordarshan (DD), India’s only channel, seemed to be like friends dropping by every evening, updating us about the nation. Sheila Chaman belongs to that fond era of DD newsreaders, whose diction and dress were imitated in equal measure.Chaman’s association with DD started earlier than her news-reading days. And its roots lay in a Weston TV bought on installments. An evening programme that caught her eye was ‘Mirror of the World’, a collection of visual snippets from across the globe. She wrote to the show’s female producer, expressing her desire to host the programme. Nobody responded. “In the last line, I mentioned in the last line that I was the winner of the 1971 Miss Young India title,” she recalls.The beauty pageant winner title — actors Shashi Kapoor and Kamini Kaushal were among the judges — got DD’s attention.The 22-year-old soon received a pink telegram, asking her to meet the producer. She was put on a single trial run. The job not only needed her to watch tapes from different embassies and cultural centres and select visual clippings, but also to memorise her lines before going on air.Chaman passed the test and became the show’s regular presenter, receiving Rs 75 for a week’s work in 1976. She would go on to host shows like ‘Panorama’ and ‘Our Guest Tonight’ before eventually becoming a newsreader.Sitting in the elegant Delhi Gymkhana, now under govt scrutiny, Chaman speaks with the poise of old, emphasising constantly the importance of flawless diction that personified DD newsreaders such as Tejeshwar Singh, Neethi Ravindran and Minu, to name a few. She talks about practicing correct pronunciation — and how tongue twisters improve fluency.“It’s like a singer does riyaaz,” she says. “Betty bought a bit of butter, but she found the butter bitter, so she bought a bit of better butter to make the bitter butter better,” the former newsreader reels out, without faltering.Back in the day, newbies read Parliament News. With most parliamentarians closely following the bulletin, names had to be pronounced correctly. It helped that Chaman knew nine languages, partly through spending her early years in southern and eastern states, where her father worked for the Union food and agriculture ministry. “I used to ring up the desk of the state guest house and ask how a name was pronounced,” she says.In the pre-autocue and -teleprompter era, reading television news was challenging, to say the least. “We read from the script, looking up and down. It was like a clutch and brake,” she says. Chaman recalls how a howler was avoided when she received a page when a bulletin was in progress that went, “Prime Minister Giani Zail Singh”. She had to make a spot decision: read it as either “Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi” or “President Giani Zail Singh”. “My gut feeling conveyed that it should be read as the latter, and so I did. It turned out to be the right call. This came as a huge relief to everyone who was on the bulletin that day,” she writes in her book, ‘Doordarshan Diaries’.On Oct 31, 1984 — the day PM Indira Gandhi was shot dead by her bodyguards, Chaman was slotted to read the evening news in English. Before her, Salma Sultan, whom she counts among her friends, read the Hindi bulletin. “I tried to keep myself as composed as possible,” Chaman says. After the news, the producer, a Sikh gentleman, was about to leave for home when he received a call from his wife. “Suddenly, his face was ashen. She told him not to come home that night. There was mayhem on the streets,” Chaman recalls. The anti-Sikh riots claimed over 2,000 lives in the national capital.On July 13, 1991, Chaman was returning from a family trip from Shirdi when a car coming from the opposite direction rammed into their Contessa. “My head hit the dashboard, and glass pieces were in my face. For about 10-15 minutes, I had no vision,” she remembers. At the Bombay hospital on Marine Lines, she underwent plastic surgery, where hundreds of micro-stitches were needed to repair her face. Six weeks on, she was back to reading news on television. But, thereafter, the newsreader decided to become a news correspondent.Chaman’s Sindhi parents — they are Chhuganis, and 60s film star Kumud Chhugani is a relative — had migrated from Sindh to Delhi during Partition. She was born in Delhi, but grew up in different cities, especially Calcutta, where she spent her Miss Young India days and did a guest role in the Bengali film ‘Chithi’ (1972). Not many may remember that she also played a doctor acting matchmaker between Dr Ashwin and Badki in the iconic DD serial ‘Hum Log’. Fewer would know that she compered shows for the Kalyanji-Anandji music troupe.What gives her the bigger satisfaction, however, is that “many successful television news anchors were briefly trained” by her. “It’s very important to have eye contact with the viewers,” she says. “More than words, you speak with your eyes and body language.”In the 80s, DD newsreaders were like celebs. But Chaman discovered at a Chandigarh lit fest last year that those of a certain vintage still remember her with affection and admiration. “It’s amazing how Doordarshan embedded us in the minds and hearts of people,” she says. Memories, as they say, are gold; and they never grow old.
Article Summary: Former DD newsreader and author, Sheila Chaman, was also Miss Young India in 1971. Chaman’s association with DD started earlier than her news-reading days. She would go on to host shows like ‘Panorama’ and ‘Our Guest Tonight’

Article Title: Modak frenzy grips NCR as Ganpati Bappa arrives
Article Text:
With the city gearing up to welcome Ganpati Bappa today, modaks are once again adding sweetness to festive tables

The modak rush

Making an ukadiche modak is a skill-intensive process, with the rice-flour dough kneaded while hot to develop the elasticity needed to shape the covering

The usual customer base is people who are getting Ganpati at home for the next couple of days.

‘Familiar in shape but contemporary in taste’

Going beyond the sweets

A festive spread beyond modaks: Vada pav, misal pav, dabeli, thalipeeth, kothimbir vadi, sabudana vada, chakli and other Maharashtrian savouries add to the Ganpati feast





Come Ganpati, come modak. As Bappa makes his way into homes across Delhi, the team is making around 1,000 modaks a day at the Maharashtra Stall in Dilli Haat INA, while home chefs and Maharashtrian food businesses are taking bulk orders for the festive sweet.Vaishali Chiplunkar, co-owner of the Maharashtra Stall says, “Every year, we hire about five to six extra people just to make the modaks, as our regular staff is always engaged in running the restaurant. On some customers’ demand, we are also doing khoya modaks. We don’t usually sell this because it is very common and you might get it anywhere.”Nishit Dalal, founder of Bombay Boy, a Maharashtrian snack outlet in Malviya Nagar, says, “Last year, we did around 150 kgs (roughly 2,400 modaks), and we expect a similar response or more this year. The usual customer base is people who are getting Ganpati at home for the next couple of days. Apart from them, people hailing from Maharashtra buy ukadiche modak to get the feel of home.”For chef Bharati Sanghi, director, Life Artisanal Food, the demand has translated into around 60-65 orders this year, with most coming in for the evening of sthapana and for chaturthi. “I make traditional ukadiche modaks every year, but this time I received relatively fewer orders for them compared to the fruit-filled variants.Most of the orders are to be delivered in Gurgaon, Golf Links, Swami Nagar, GK 1 and GK 2,” she says. Malti Vig of Malti’s Kitchen, a home chef based in Gurgaon, has also received bulk orders. “This year, a Noida resident ordered 100 boxes, while someone from Vasant Kunj ordered 50.”Traditionally made with rice flour and filled with coconut and jaggery, the modak has now become a canvas for experimentation. Bharati is doing an apple-filled variant. “I am experimenting with the filling while still retaining the traditional modak form. I am also doing blueberry and cranberry variants. The idea was to give people something familiar in shape and festive in spirit, but unexpected and contemporary in taste,” she says. Malti, too, makes the steamed variety, alongside the khoya ones in flavours including paan and strawberry.The Ganpati spread goes beyond the sweet, with Maharashtrian savouries also finding their way into festive orders, family gatherings and bhog.Dr Bhagyeshwari of Gurgaon-based Dr B’s Theplas & Dhoklas says, “There are three important things which people are ordering this Bappa’s season — modaks, puran poli and churma laddu. We have made special arrangements in terms of our team to cater to the festive orders. Apart from modaks, puran poli and shakarpara, we also have snacks such as chakli and vada pav, and we do get orders for these as well. If there is a Ganpati gathering at somebody’s place, they give us party orders for these snacks. ”At the Maharashtra Sadan, the savoury spread includes kothimbir vadi, alu, misal, vada pav, sabudana vada, pudachi vadi
Article Summary: The usual customer base is people who are getting Ganpati at home for the next couple of days. Maharashtrian savouries are also finding their way into festive orders, family gatherings and bhog. Most of the orders are to be delivered in Gurgaon, Golf Links, Swami Nagar, GK 1 and GK 2.

Article Title: Jamia students’ protest over hostel food continues, univ says it’s fast-tracking process
Article Text:
TOI

Paise poore lete hain, khana ganda dete hain





New Delhi: The protest by women students of Jamia Millia Islamia over insects allegedly found in hostel food entered its third day Saturday, with protesters alleging that the administration had failed to honour assurances given to them earlier.The protest, led by residents of J&K Girls’ Hostel, began Thursday night and continued till around 3am Friday. Students had demanded immediate cancellation of the contract of the current mess vendor, deployment of only women staff in the mess and protection against retaliatory action against protesters.The administration then gave them a written assurance that the vendor’s contract would be terminated with immediate effect and agreed to the other two demands, following which the protest was called off.The university earlier said the process to remove the vendor would take some time as the existing contractor would need to shift his stocks and utensils.However, students alleged that the administration later reneged on the assurance, claiming that the contract had not been cancelled and another person from the same team had been appointed as manager. Students also alleged that their names and roll numbers were taken down Friday afternoon before they were served meals, raising fears of retaliatory action.The protest resumed Friday and continued Saturday, with women students from other hostels joining the agitation and male students also extending solidarity.The university denied the allegations that it had failed to honour its assurances. “Issuing a tender for a mess contractor in a govt institution has a due process that needs to be followed. We have fast-tracked the process and, as an interim arrangement, are arranging food from another vendor for the students,” chief public relations officer Saima Saeed toldSaturday.Protesting near Centenary Gate, students raised slogans such as “”. Friday night, they stayed at the gate, defying the hostel curfew, and alleged that the lights at the site were switched off. They switched on their phone flashlights and banged plates in protest.Meanwhile, the main entrance to the hostel remained locked Saturday, students said, sharing a video of the locked gate. They later entered through another gate and were not stopped, they said.A protester said students were worried about their sessional examinations beginning Monday. The delay in resolving the issue is increasing pressure on protesters to call off the agitation, she alleged.
Article Summary: The protest, led by residents of J&K Girls’ Hostel, began Thursday night and continued till around 3am Friday. Students demanded immediate cancellation of the contract of the current mess vendor, deployment of only women staff in the mess and protection against retaliatory action.
